# OSS Verify: proofs about OSS-Fuzz fuzz targets

[![release-check](https://github.com/theorem-labs/oss-verify-proofs/actions/workflows/release-check.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/theorem-labs/oss-verify-proofs/actions/workflows/release-check.yml?query=branch%3Amain)

OSS-Fuzz runs the fuzz targets of open-source projects to search for inputs that make them fail. This repository holds Rocq proofs that, for some of these fuzz targets, no such input exists within stated limits. Each proof is about compiled binaries, not source code. It shows that, on every input within the limits, the build with a sanitizer behaves like the plain build and the sanitizer never detects an error, or that every execution of a build ends with a status the statement allows. OSS Verify is a Theorem program; a maintainer enrolls a project at [theorem-labs/oss-verify](https://github.com/theorem-labs/oss-verify).

90 entry points in 32 libraries have proofs. The proofs are checked with Rocq 9.2.0. They are stated in LPS, a formal model of a Linux process that runs a RISC-V binary.

**LPS is best effort and not complete.** It describes part of Linux, and it makes some assumptions that it does not check. A proof is only as good as LPS. [docs/semantics.md](docs/semantics.md) gives the design principles of LPS and its limits.

Every proof is about the binaries of this release and the statements under `projects/`. All of them use one LPS version and one static AddressSanitizer ([Versions](#versions)). [docs/origin.md](docs/origin.md) says how the proofs were made: the proving task, its submissions and its checker, and how a proof enters this repository.

## The theorem, in words
Every proof here proves one or more agreement statements, halts statements, or both. There is one agreement statement for each sanitizer build: AddressSanitizer (ASan), UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan), or both (ASan+UBSan). An agreement statement says:

> On every input on which the plain build stays within its memory budget, neither build reaches an error, and the plain build and the sanitizer build have the same set of observable behaviours.

- **Every input** means every process input that LPS accepts as valid: the arguments, the environment variables, the files (so the input file, its contents or its absence), standard input, and the rest of what a process receives. LPS leaves out a few inputs; for example, an argument after the program name may not contain `/` ([docs/semantics.md](docs/semantics.md)).
- **An error** is a crash, an invalid memory access, an `abort()` (a failed `assert()`, a sanitizer report or an uncaught C++ exception), a failed UBSan check, or a step that LPS does not interpret. In a Rust fuzz target, a failed rustc UB check is not an error: it exits with status 79 after a line on standard error that the plain build does not write at that point, so agreement rules it out too.
- **Observable behaviours** are the bytes that the process reads and writes on its standard streams and connections, in order, its exit status, and the final contents of its files.
- **The memory budget** of the plain build is 2 GiB in a statement about a build with ASan (ASan or ASan+UBSan), and 16 GiB in a statement about the UBSan build. The budget is a premise: an input on which the plain build needs more memory is not covered.
- **System-call failures.** Each statement says which system calls the environment may refuse without cause. In most of the proofs here, a memory request is refused only when the budget is spent or no address range is free.

So an agreement proof rules out every error that the sanitizer build detects, on every input that the statement covers.

A halts statement is about one build alone. It says that on every covered input, every execution of that build ends, and that it ends with a status the statement allows: status 0 or 2 for most harnesses, status 0, 2 or 78 for a harness that lists the inputs it turns away (`rejects`), and any status for espeak-ng's `ssml-fuzzer`. Its premises are its own: the build is never refused memory for exceeding 16 GiB, and the environment refuses nothing that the process's state does not force. A `_halts_may_fail` statement drops both premises and allows any status.

If the harness checks a property with `assert()`, `abort()` or a trap, and the check is in the binary, an agreement proof shows that the property holds on every covered input. A halts proof shows it only for the checks that the fuzz target's page names: a check seen in the binary, of a fuzz target whose linked code installs no handler that could end a failed check with a status of its own (`failure_handlers: none`). A failed check of these kinds then kills the process, which no halts statement allows. A check that ends the process with `exit()` instead is shown only when the call reaches the driver's exit guard (`exit_reaches_guard: true`), which ends the process with status 77 whatever status the source passes, and only by a halts statement whose allowed statuses leave out 77 ([docs/facts.md](docs/facts.md), [docs/exploring.md](docs/exploring.md), [docs/statements.md](docs/statements.md)).

The Rocq definitions are in [theories/Shapes.v](theories/Shapes.v). Each agreement and halts form is proved equal to its LPS definition: an agreement form to `strong_universal_error_free_T_budgets` or one of its variants, a halts form to `halts_allowed_T_scfg_budgets` or `halts_allowed_T_scfg`. [docs/statements.md](docs/statements.md) explains each form.

## What a proof does not say
- It does not say that the library is correct. Errors that the sanitizers cannot detect are not excluded: for example, a wrong result or a memory leak.
- It is about the code that one entry point reaches, not about the whole library.
- It is about these binaries: static riscv64 programs, built with clang 20.1.8 against musl. It is not about the source code, and not about the x86-64 builds of OSS-Fuzz.
- It is true in LPS. Where LPS differs from Linux, the proof may not apply ([docs/semantics.md](docs/semantics.md)).
- An agreement statement does not exclude a run that never ends. Only a halts statement does. 179 of the proved statements are halts statements; [index/PROOFS.md](index/PROOFS.md) lists them.

## Check a proof
You need Docker, zstd, and Python 3 with the packages `tools/oft/requirements.txt` pins (PyYAML; for `./oft lint`, also idna). The checker image holds Rocq and LPS, but not PyYAML, so the commands below mount it. On 16 cores, one proof check needs up to 20 GiB of memory. It compiles one file per core, so more cores need more memory; `docker run --cpuset-cpus` limits the cores. `--ulimit stack=-1:-1` gives the container an unlimited stack hard limit, so the check gets the 2 GiB stack it asks for; under a lower limit it still runs, with less stack, and it prints the stack it got ([docs/checking.md](docs/checking.md#stack-size)).

    git clone https://github.com/theorem-labs/oss-verify-proofs && cd oss-verify-proofs
    ./oft fetch coturn                   # the project's binaries, each checked against its SHA-256
    python3 -m pip install --require-hashes --target "$HOME/oft-pydeps" -r tools/oft/requirements.txt
    docker run --rm --network none --ulimit stack=-1:-1 -u "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp -e PYTHONPATH=/pydeps \
      -v "$HOME/oft-pydeps:/pydeps:ro" -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work ghcr.io/theorem-labs/oss-fuzz-theorems-checker@sha256:063f93261f11ba449f1c3825884fadc65cf1fc836d4a3ee534633211abbdc3eb \
      ./oft check coturn/FuzzStunClient --parts statements,proofs

`oft check` does these steps. It checks each binary against its SHA-256. It builds the memory images and the statements. It compiles each proof. It compiles a small wrapper that gives the proof's theorem the type of the statement. Then it reads what `Print Assumptions` prints for the wrapper, and it refuses every assumption that is not in the allowed list ([docs/checking.md](docs/checking.md)).

CI runs the same check. The [release-check](.github/workflows/release-check.yml) workflow checks what each push to `main` changes, and the badge at the top shows its result. The [pr](.github/workflows/pr.yml) workflow checks what a pull request changes. A publication checks the parts whose content keys it changes. Every Monday the [weekly](.github/workflows/weekly.yml) workflow checks every statement and every proof, with no cache; after a release, it also checks the fuzz targets of the projects whose files that release attached ([docs/checking.md](docs/checking.md#what-ci-runs)).

## How the binaries are built
Each binary is a static riscv64 Linux program, built with clang 20.1.8 against musl. An entry point has up to four builds: plain, ASan, UBSan and ASan+UBSan. [docs/building.md](docs/building.md) gives the compiler flags and the sanitizer settings. [docs/running.md](docs/running.md) tells you how to run a binary and what its input file holds.

Each proof has a build record in `projects/<project>/<harness>/proofs/provenance/`. The record gives the upstream repository and commit, the harness file, the recipe (for a port-built project, the OSS Verify port's build manifest and its files for the project), the compiler, the builder image, the static AddressSanitizer commit, the compiler and linker flags, the SHA-256 of each binary, and the licences. [docs/reproducing.md](docs/reproducing.md) tells you how to rebuild a binary and compare its SHA-256.

Each project's published binaries are attached to the [release](https://github.com/theorem-labs/oss-verify-proofs/releases) as one archive, and each binary is pinned by its SHA-256 in its `harness.yaml`. Where a recipe-built project's page names them, the project's upstream source trees are attached with the build recipe its binaries were built with, in the releases the page links (the source trees beside the binaries, or in a second release, `v<release>-src`, since a GitHub release holds at most 1,000 files); together they rebuild the binaries ([docs/reproducing.md](docs/reproducing.md)). A port-built project's page names its source trees and its port archive when it attaches them, as it must for a GPL or LGPL binary; the port archive holds the port's build scripts and the source of the driver in its binaries. The port's `tools/check` builds them again with Docker and fetches the source trees over the network, not from the attached archive ([docs/reproducing.md](docs/reproducing.md)).

## Explore the proofs
[docs/exploring.md](docs/exploring.md) points to what the proofs show beyond "no sanitizer error": properties that the harnesses check, and lemmas about what the library code computes. It also tells you how to find the machine-generated data in a proof.

## Statements for OSS-Fuzz fuzz targets
This repository also states theorems about many OSS-Fuzz fuzz targets, proved or not. For each of the 1,381 projects in OSS-Fuzz there is a directory under [projects/](projects/). It also has project directories for [`libdiginet`](projects/libdiginet/), [`libreac`](projects/libreac/), [`omx-clap-core`](projects/omx-clap-core/), [`omx-dsp`](projects/omx-dsp/), [`plugin-hostd`](projects/plugin-hostd/), [`reac-pw`](projects/reac-pw/) and [`reac-repacer`](projects/reac-repacer/); OSS-Fuzz has no project for them. We can build the fuzz targets of 427 of these projects. 2,148 of their 5,290 fuzz targets have statements in this release; [index/STATUS.md](index/STATUS.md) says why the others do not. Each of these fuzz targets is compiled up to four ways (2,176 of the 2,183 harnesses have all four), and each build gets Rocq statements about those exact bytes. These are statements, not results: 526 are proved, some are known to be false, and proofs are added as they are found.

In this release: 20,421 statements: 526 proved, 7 known false (0 counterexamples, 7 false (witnessed)), 3 suspected false, 229 blocked by the model, 0 withheld (0 waiting for their source bundle, 0 not published yet), 19,656 open. [analyses/known-issues.md](analyses/known-issues.md) lists every statement that is not open or proved, with the reason.

There are four kinds of statement: a build halts; a sanitizer build agrees with the plain build; the two builds disagree on at most a fraction *b* of a stated input distribution; and the inputs on which they agree are decidable ([docs/statements.md](docs/statements.md)). One example:

[`lzo/lzo_compress_target/plain_halts`](projects/lzo/lzo_compress_target/Statements.v): on every input on which the plain build is never refused memory for exceeding 16 GiB, and when the environment refuses nothing that it is not forced to (both are premises), every execution exits with status 0 or 2. The harness `lzo_compress_target` asserts that for compressible input (compressed_len < size), lzo1x_decompress into size+1 bytes must return LZO_E_OK and produce exactly size bytes. ONLY THE LENGTH is compared: the decompressed content is never memcmp'd against the input, so a decoder that returned the right number of wrong bytes would pass, so a proof shows that these hold on every input it covers.

    Definition plain_halts : Prop :=
      halts_within_budget Budgets.Standard.lim_source Exits.ok_or_refused Images.plain.

The 434 available projects have 2,183 harnesses with statements and 20,421 statements; 8,718 binaries are attached to this release or an earlier one, and 0 more are withheld. [index/STATUS.md](index/STATUS.md) lists every project; `index/*.tsv` has the same data for scripts.

To prove or refute a statement, see [docs/proving.md](docs/proving.md) and [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). A counterexample that shows a bug in a library goes to that library first ([SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md)). To enroll your own project, see [theorem-labs/oss-verify](https://github.com/theorem-labs/oss-verify).

## What you have to trust
- The Rocq kernel, with its bytecode machine (`vm_compute`), and the axioms in [toolchain/allowed-axioms.txt](toolchain/allowed-axioms.txt).
- LPS, at the commit that [release.yaml](release.yaml) names ([docs/semantics.md](docs/semantics.md)).
- The tools that turn an ELF file into an LPS memory image: LPS's `elf-snapshot`, and `rocq-read-file` 0.0.2, an OCaml plugin that reads the image's bytes into Rocq at compile time.
- `oft check`: the wrapper that it writes, and its reading of `Print Assumptions` ([tools/oft/check.py](tools/oft/check.py)).

[docs/trust.md](docs/trust.md) says what each of these covers.

## Repository layout
| path | contents |
|---|---|
| `projects/<project>/<harness>/` | the facts (`harness.yaml`), the statements (`Statements.v`), the images (`Images.v`), the harness page, and, for most harnesses, a copy of the harness source (`source/`) |
| `projects/<project>/<harness>/proofs/<statement>/` | the proof of one statement, and its `proof.yaml` |
| `projects/<project>/<harness>/proofs/provenance/` | the build record of that harness's binaries |
| `projects/<project>/<harness>/proofs/lib/` | the lemmas that the proofs of that harness share |
| `theories/` | the statement forms (`Shapes.v`), the image library, and the input-file format (`Driver.v`) |
| `index/` | tables of every proof, project, harness, statement and binary |
| `toolchain/` | the Dockerfiles of the checker and runner images, which [release.yaml](release.yaml) pins by digest, the allowed axioms, and the list of LPS files |
| `tools/oft/` | the `oft` tool: fetch, generate, lint and check |
| `tests/` | a generator of toy binaries, and controls that the checker must accept or refuse |
| `projects/<project>/<harness>/counterexamples/` | inputs that make a binary break a statement, each with a control input |
| `analyses/` | the checks that the harnesses make (`harness-checks/`), and every statement that is not open or proved (`known-issues.md`) |
| `LICENSES/` | licence texts of proof files made from proofs under another licence |
| `docs/` | the documentation |

## Citing
[CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff). A statement is cited as `project/harness/statement@r<revision>`, for example `lzo/lzo_compress_target/plain_halts@r1`. Until LPS is released, revisions are provisional ([docs/versioning.md](docs/versioning.md)).
